Battle of Guadalcanal. Fought from August nineteen forty-two to February nineteen forty-three, Guadalcanal was the first major ground offensive launched by the Allies in the Pacific. American forces, seeking to prevent Japanese consolidation of the Solomon Islands, secured the airfield and gradually overcame determined Japanese resistance in a grueling six-month campaign that tested American logistics and resolve.

The campaign lasted six months, with the island airfield codenamed Henderson Field becoming the strategic prize. American forces initially landed with one Marine division under Major General Alexander Vandegrift and were reinforced by Army units. Japanese commander General Hyakutake reinforced the garrison repeatedly, leading to numerous failed counteroffensives. The Japanese lost over twenty-four thousand soldiers, while American losses were approximately sixteen hundred killed and forty-two hundred wounded. This disparity reflected American superiority in logistics and reinforcement capacity.

Naval engagements raged throughout the campaign, including the Battle of the Coral Sea, Savo Island, and Tassafaronga, with both sides suffering carrier and destroyer losses. The U.S. victory established a foothold for future advances up the Solomon Islands chain toward the Philippines and demonstrated an American industrial advantage—the ability to replace ships, aircraft, and troops faster than Japan could replace its losses, a crucial advantage that preceded the later battles at Tarawa and Saipan.
